evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid Iranian-American teacher’s cat becomes the vessel for an ancient demon, forcing him to save his family from a supernatural bloodline curse before it kills everyone he loves.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The cat-as-demon hook is instantly legible and easy to sell, and the family-cursed-by-a-supernatural-force engine gives the movie a clean emotional promise. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant horror breakout because the script leans hard into Jewish-Iranian family specificity and dense mythology, but the premise is still very marketable.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: Ben wakes up with Cletus on his chest, then the script quickly reveals the cat is tied to a demon that moves through the family. By the time Neda’s condition, the red eyes, and the violent deaths stack up, the premise is unmistakable.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ben is a strong lead because he’s soft, funny, ashamed, and finally forced into action, while Holly and Darius give the movie a lively support system. The characters are appealing, but the script is more built around Ben’s emotional journey than around a deeply surprising ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a wild tonal mashup: domestic breakup comedy, Jewish family drama, occult lore, and full-body horror set pieces. The cat possession angle and the specific demon mythology give it a fresh commercial identity rather than a generic exorcism template.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the deaths start, the movie keeps escalating with clear cause-and-effect and increasingly outrageous set pieces. The middle section does spend time on lore and family exposition, but the story keeps re-arming itself with new threats and reversals.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The premise feels both strange and inevitable: a cat becomes the vessel for a family-devouring demon, and the emotional center is a grandson trying to save his grandmother’s soul. That combination of intimate family loss and absurdly specific horror is memorable in a way that should travel.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a textured world of Jewish ritual objects, demon lore, family history, and occult protection tools, and it uses the apartment, gallery, shop, and family homes as extensions of that world. It’s rich, though the mythology is more functional than deeply layered.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is unusually specific: affectionate family banter, queer and straight romantic tension, deadpan jokes, and then sudden grotesque body horror. That tonal confidence is one of the script’s biggest assets.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the horror engine is a real story about inheritance, grief, memory loss, and the fear of losing family before they’re gone. The Neda/Adir material and Ben’s unresolved father wound give the script more emotional depth than the premise initially suggests.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ben, Darius, Holly, Neda, Farah, Cyra, Tristian, Mina, Aaron, and the cops all generate distinct relational energy, and the family dynamics are story-generating on their own. The Ben/Darius/Holly triangle plus the larger Shirazi/Torkan family web gives the movie a strong ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Ben Shirazi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, Iranian American, engaged/then newly single, emotionally avoidant, aspiring writer and teacher.
lead_characters.hook: Ben is a gentle, self-effacing guy who has spent years being the nice one in every room, until a breakup, his grandmother’s dementia, and a demon in his cat force him to become the adult in the family. He’s funny without trying, wounded without being precious, and the script keeps finding new ways to test whether his softness is a liability or his superpower.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Adam Driver or Jake Johnson-type performance in a horror-comedy lead — someone who can play embarrassment, yearning, and panic without losing likability. The role gives an actor a full arc from passive romantic loser to terrified protector, with emotional close-ups, comic timing, and a late-film hero turn.

lead_characters.name: Holly Martin
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 30s, Caucasian, cosmopolitan, occult-informed, owner of a metaphysical shop.
lead_characters.hook: Holly is the script’s smartest practical mind: a former student turned friend who knows the occult rules, but never loses her warmth or dry humor. She’s competent without becoming cold, and the script lets her be both the audience’s explainer and Ben’s emotional counterweight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded authority of Allison Williams in Get Out or Rebecca Hall in The Night House — the person who can carry exposition because the performance has trust and intelligence. It also offers a romantic charge and a late-film action/ritual payoff.

lead_characters.name: Darius Walker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, African American, handsome, buff, openly affectionate, Ben’s best friend.
lead_characters.hook: Darius is the movie’s pressure-release valve and emotional ballast, but he’s not just comic relief; he’s the friend who keeps Ben from collapsing into self-pity. He’s funny, physically confident, and unexpectedly tender, with a real sense of loyalty that makes the friendship feel lived-in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of best-friend role that lets an actor do the easy charisma of Lakeith Stanfield in a lighter register or the grounded warmth of Brian Tyree Henry in ensemble mode. It gives a performer banter, physical presence, and a few scenes of real emotional support.

lead_characters.name: Neda Shirazi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 70s, Iranian American, professor/writer, sharp-tongued, later cognitively impaired.
lead_characters.hook: Neda is the heart of the family and the movie’s most poignant contradiction: a brilliant, commanding woman whose mind is slipping just as the supernatural threat closes in. She’s funny, proud, difficult, loving, and heartbreaking, and the script gives her a tragic dignity even when the demon is using her body as a battleground.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige character-actor territory in the vein of June Squibb in Nebraska or Frances Sternhagen in a late-career showcase — a role that lets an actor be formidable, comic, and devastating. The dementia material plus the possession material creates a rare double-performance opportunity.

lead_characters.name: Jillian Napier
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 20s, Caucasian, petite, sharp, emotionally done with the relationship.
lead_characters.hook: Jillian is not a villain so much as the person who says the thing Ben has been avoiding: he has not built a life, only a habit. She’s cutting, funny, and practical, and the script uses her breakup as the emotional detonator that sends Ben into the main story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the sharp, unsentimental breakup energy of a Greta Gerwig or Kathryn Hahn scene-part — the person who can land a whole relationship history in a few lines. It’s a compact but memorable part with real bite.

lead_characters.name: Kallie Douglas
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 40s, Caucasian, tough detective, no-nonsense, skeptical.
lead_characters.hook: Kallie is the procedural anchor in a movie that keeps trying to outrun logic. She’s skeptical, sharp, and increasingly trapped between evidence and the impossible, which gives the police thread a nice grounded friction.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong detective material in the mold of Carrie Coon or Regina King in a grounded genre piece — a role that lets an actor play authority, skepticism, and dawning dread. The best scenes are the ones where she has to keep a straight face while reality gets stranger.

lead_characters.name: Esteban Cruz
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid 30s, Latino, muscular, handsome, detective, emotionally open.
lead_characters.hook: Esteban is Kallie’s partner and the movie’s most openly flirtatious adult male presence outside the central friend group. He’s competent, funny, and increasingly willing to believe the impossible, which makes him a useful bridge between the cops and the occult crew.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the easy charm of Michael Peña in a genre ensemble — a part that can play banter, action, and a little romantic spark. It’s not huge, but it’s very playable.

lead_characters.name: Farah Torkan
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 50s, Iranian American, wealthy, conservative, protective daughter and mother.
lead_characters.hook: Farah is the family member who tries hardest to keep the house respectable while everything around her becomes spiritually and emotionally unmanageable. Her grief, guilt, and maternal panic give the family drama real weight, especially once the demon starts weaponizing her memories.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do contained devastation in the style of Shohreh Aghdashloo or a strong prestige-drama matriarch. The possession/hallucination material gives her a real breakdown showcase.

lead_characters.name: Cyra Tate
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 70s, Iranian American, glamorous, vain, resentful, socially sharp.
lead_characters.hook: Cyra is all brittle elegance and old grudges, which makes her a great pressure point in the family web. She’s funny, catty, and emotionally compromised, and the script lets her become both a comic irritant and a horror victim.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a delicious character-actor part in the vein of Judith Light or Margo Martindale — a role that lets an actor be sharp, vain, wounded, and then terrifyingly vulnerable. The vampire delusion sequence gives it a wild swing.

lead_characters.name: Mina Shirazi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 50s, Iranian American, bitter, emotionally guarded, Ben’s mother.
lead_characters.hook: Mina is a hard, defensive mother whose love is buried under resentment and old family damage. The demon sequence turns that buried pain into something brutal and tragic, making her one of the script’s most painful emotional casualties.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a late-film emotional gut punch in the tradition of a strong family-drama supporting turn. The hallucination/possessed confrontation is the showcase.

lead_characters.name: Aaron Shirazi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid 20s, Iranian American, overweight, shy, sexually repressed.
lead_characters.hook: Aaron is the family’s overlooked oddball, and the script uses him to show how much shame and loneliness can live under the surface of a household. His private life is played for shock and comedy, but the character also reads as deeply isolated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a risky but memorable supporting part in the vein of a scene-stealing indie oddball role — the kind that can make an actor unforgettable if they commit fully. It’s a bold swing with a lot of specificity.

casting_characteristics: ensemble with several Iranian American family roles
one lead role that must carry comedy, romance, and horror

technical.vfx_details: Mirror mist, demon manifestations, hallucination overlays, Grimalkin transformation, Lilith vulture reveal, and a few large supernatural set pieces.
technical.sfx_needs: Heavy practical gore, blood rigs, prosthetic wounds, body horror effects, and creature makeup/puppet work for Grimalkin and Cletus moments.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a streamer-friendly genre title or specialty theatrical horror-comedy.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the creature work, heavy gore, multiple supernatural transformations, and Death Valley finale push this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Ben has to carry romantic comedy, family drama, and escalating horror, while Neda needs a performer who can play wit, authority, and dementia with real precision.

development.note: The mythology is clear enough to follow, but the script asks the audience to track a lot of family history, demon rules, and hallucination logic while still staying emotionally invested.

comp_set.title: The Voices
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the darkly comic, psychologically unstable horror-comedy lane and the idea of a pet becoming the engine of escalating violence.

comp_set.title: Ready or Not
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the propulsive genre escalation, family-in-peril structure, and crowd-pleasing blend of bloodshed with jokes.

comp_set.title: The Night House
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on grief-driven supernatural dread and the way the emotional wound is inseparable from the haunting.

comp_set.title: A Ghost Story
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not on genre mechanics, but on the emotional relationship to loss, memory, and the dead remaining present.

comp_set.title: Shiva Baby
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the Jewish-family specificity, social discomfort, and pressure-cooker family dynamics, even though this script goes fully supernatural.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated horror with a strong comic edge, plus viewers drawn to family-specific stories and creature-driven genre swings.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly male-leaning on the horror side but with strong female appeal through the family and relationship material; urban and streamer-native audiences especially likely.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations keep it contained, but the creature effects, gore, and Death Valley finale keep it in the upper indie lane.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals execs building elevated-horror slates
specialty distributors looking for a crowd-pleasing midnight title
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where a strong hook, a distinctive voice, and a manageable production footprint can coexist. The family specificity and cat-demon premise give it a clean marketing angle without requiring a tentpole budget.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a complete emotional and supernatural arc; the ending teases Lilith, but there is no clear franchise engine or spinoff character with separate-project depth.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The cat-demon hook is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the movie a one-sentence marketing engine that is weird, funny, and scary at the same time. Buyers looking for a high-concept horror title can understand the sell immediately, and horror audiences know exactly what kind of ride they’re getting.
strengths.evidence: Cletus starts as a cuddly house cat, then becomes the vessel for Grimalkin and the source of the family deaths.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family grief is baked into the horror.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie is not just about a demon; it’s about memory loss, inheritance, and the terror of losing family twice. That gives the script emotional stickiness and broadens the appeal beyond pure gore fans to viewers who want feeling with their genre.
strengths.evidence: Neda’s Alzheimer’s, Ben’s unresolved father wound, and the final choice to leave the dead behind all tie the supernatural to loss.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ben is a strong, castable lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The role can launch or reframe a young actor because it asks for comedy, vulnerability, romantic frustration, and eventual heroism. That makes the package more attractive to talent reps and to buyers who want a performance-forward genre movie.
strengths.evidence: Ben goes from breakup humiliation to occult investigator to the man who literally enters Hell for his grandmother.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble gives the movie recurring energy.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has enough distinct family and friend dynamics that scenes can keep generating tension even when the plot pauses for exposition. That’s valuable commercially because it makes the movie feel bigger than a single-protagonist scare machine.
strengths.evidence: Ben, Darius, Holly, Neda, Farah, Cyra, Mina, Aaron, Kallie, and Esteban all have distinct relational functions.

strengths.what_it_means: The script can sell itself as a horror-comedy with real emotional stakes rather than a generic possession movie. That tonal control is what makes the project feel like a director’s movie and a buyer-friendly genre swing at the same time.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from breakup jokes and family banter to grotesque body horror without losing its voice.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable elevated-horror package: a cat-demon hook, a castable male lead, and a family grief engine that gives the genre material real emotional weight. The contemporary footprint and mostly interior design keep it in indie territory, while the tone and set pieces make it feel bigger than the budget.

items.area: The mythology gets dense in the middle.
items.detail: Once the script moves from the breakup setup into demon lore, bloodline history, and ritual mechanics, the movie asks the audience to track a lot of rules while the body count is still building. That’s not a fatal issue, but it is the main friction point for broad accessibility.

items.area: The supporting cast is vivid but not franchise-deep.
items.detail: Holly, Darius, Kallie, Esteban, and the family members all pop, but the movie is still structurally Ben’s story. That keeps the ensemble lively, but it also means the project reads as a standalone feature rather than something with obvious extension value.

items.area: The gore level is a buyer filter.
items.detail: The Levi staircase death, Van’s worm sequence, Aaron’s decapitation, and the Farah self-stabbing sequence push the movie into very graphic territory. That’s a strength for horror fans, but it narrows the room on the buyer side and will shape how the title is positioned.

items.area: Ben’s romantic triangle is secondary to the horror engine.
items.detail: The Jillian breakup and Holly attraction give the lead emotional texture, but the movie quickly becomes about possession and family survival. Buyers will see the romance as flavor rather than as a second commercial engine.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise — it’s the amount of mythology the script asks the audience to absorb before the horror payoff fully locks in. The other notable buyer conversation is the graphic gore level, which is effective but clearly places the movie in a narrower genre lane.
